title: Ch 7 — Entropy
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 7
description: Entropy, the increase principle, T ds relations, and isentropic processes.

cards.back: $\displaystyle\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$ for any cycle. Equality holds for internally reversible cycles; this inequality is the basis for defining entropy.
$dS = \left(\dfrac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_{int,rev}$ (kJ/K). Entropy is a property, so $\Delta S$ between two states is independent of the path.
The entropy of an isolated system can never decrease: $S_{gen} \ge 0$. $S_{gen} = 0$ for reversible processes, $> 0$ for irreversible ones; $S_{gen} < 0$ is impossible.

cards.front: Entropy of a saturated liquid–vapor mixture?
cards.back: Like other properties: $s = s_f + x\,s_{fg}$, read from the saturation tables.

cards.front: Entropy change of an ideal gas (constant specific heats)?
What is an *isentropic* process and what is it used to model?
cards.back: A reversible and adiabatic process, for which $\Delta s = 0$. It is the ideal benchmark for adiabatic turbines, compressors, pumps and nozzles.

cards.front: Isentropic relations for an ideal gas (constant specific heats)?
Entropy change of liquids and solids (incompressible)?
cards.back: $\Delta s = c\,\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$. An isentropic process of an incompressible substance is therefore also isothermal.
$w_{rev} = -\displaystyle\int_1^2 v\,dP$ (plus ΔKE, ΔPE). For incompressible flow this gives $w_{rev} = -v(P_2 - P_1) - \Delta ke - \Delta pe$.

cards.front: A thermal reservoir at 500 K receives 1000 kJ of heat. What is its entropy change (kJ/K)?
Entropy change of an ideal gas with **variable** specific heats (large ΔT)?
cards.back: $s_2 - s_1 = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}$, where $s^\circ(T) = \int_0^T c_p\,dT/T$ is read straight from the ideal-gas table (A-17). Use this instead of constant-$c_p$ when the temperature change is large.

cards.front: For an **isentropic** ideal-gas process with variable specific heats, how do you relate the end states?
cards.back: Use the tabulated **relative pressure** and **relative specific volume** (functions of $T$ only): $\left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)_s = \dfrac{P_{r2}}{P_{r1}}$ and $\left(\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}\right)_s = \dfrac{v_{r2}}{v_{r1}}$. Read $P_{r1}/v_{r1}$ at $T_1$, scale by the ratio, read $T_2$ back off the table.

cards.front: Reversible work to compress an ideal gas — isentropic vs isothermal?
cards.back: Isentropic: $w = \dfrac{kRT_1}{k-1}\left[(P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k} - 1\right]$. Isothermal: $w = RT\ln(P_2/P_1)$. Isothermal costs the **least** work (cooling keeps $v$ small); isentropic the most.

cards.front: Optimal intermediate pressure for two-stage compression with intercooling?
cards.back: $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$ — the geometric mean. This makes the pressure ratio (and the work) equal across both stages, minimizing total work. Cooling between stages shrinks $v$ in stage 2.
$\eta_N = \dfrac{\text{actual exit KE}}{\text{isentropic exit KE}} = \dfrac{V_{2a}^2}{V_{2s}^2} = \dfrac{h_1 - h_{2a}}{h_1 - h_{2s}}$. So the actual exit velocity is $V_{2a} = \sqrt{\eta_N}\,V_{2s}$.
